Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Dual-Target Inhibition of Puumala Virus Entry Glycoproteins Gn and Gc by Moringa oleifera -Derived Phytochemicals: An Integrated Computational Study
papers.abstract: Puumala virus (PUUV), a member of the Orthohantavirus genus, causes nephropathia epidemica, an intermediate type of hemorrhagic fever with renal dysfunction, yet no approved antiviral therapy is currently available. Viral entry is initiated by the coordinated actions of the attachment glycoprotein Gn and fusion glycoprotein Gc, making simultaneous inhibition of these proteins an attractive antiviral strategy. Here, we employed a combined computational workflow to identify dual-target inhibitors of PUUV entry glycoproteins from Moringa oleifera phytochemicals. 72 phytochemicals were retrieved and docked by molecular docking to identify high-affinity binders, while he top-ranked compounds were subsequently evaluated for drug-likeness, pharmacokinetic behavior, toxicity, and predicted biological activities to assess their therapeutic suitability. Complex stability and binding mechanisms were further investigated through 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations (MDS) and MM-GBSA binding free-energy calculations. Quercetin and kaempferol showed the lowest binding energies toward Gn (−9.8 and −9.7 kcal/mol) and Gc (−10.4 and −10.0 kcal/mol), respectively. Both phytochemicals demonstrated favorable drug-like properties, high gastrointestinal absorption, no predicted toxicity, and positive bioactivity scores. MDS confirmed stable protein–ligand complexes with minimal structural fluctuations, and MM-GBSA analysis further validated strong binding, with quercetin exhibiting the most favorable binding free energies against Gn (−84.24 kcal/mol) and Gc (−98.45 kcal/mol). These findings identify quercetin and kaempferol as promising dual-target inhibitors that may simultaneously disrupt PUUV attachment and membrane fusion, warranting further experimental validation.

Both phytochemicals demonstrated favorable drug-like properties, high gastrointestinal absorption, no predicted toxicity, and positive bioactivity scores. MDS confirmed stable protein–ligand complexes with minimal structural fluctuations, and MM-GBSA analysis further validated strong binding, with quercetin exhibiting the most favorable binding free energies against Gn (−84.24 kcal/mol) and Gc (−98.45 kcal/mol). These findings identify quercetin and kaempferol as promising dual-target inhibitors that may simultaneously disrupt PUUV attachment and membrane fusion, warranting further experimental validation.

papers.title: Prediction of Quercetin as a Potential Modulator of HTNV-Related Host Responses: An Integrated Computational Study with Baseline Pharmacological Characterization
papers.abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that is mainly distributed in East Asia. It is a typical example of a One Health challenge, because it persists in rodent reservoirs without causing disease in the animals but causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) when it infects humans. This study employed an integrated bioinformatics approach to systematically identify early-stage HTNV-related host interaction factors, screen potential natural compounds, and predict their underlying therapeutic mechanisms. Integrative bioinformatics analysis identified CXCL10, STAT1, and IL10 as the principal upregulated core genes associated with early-stage HTNV infection. Based on these targets, six candidate natural compounds were retrieved from the HERB database. Notably, quercetin emerged as the most promising candidate, exhibiting a favorable pharmacological profile characterized by high predicted gastrointestinal absorption and an acceptable predicted toxicity profile based on in silico ADMET assessment. Functional enrichment of HTNV-related host interaction targets suggested that HTNV infection may affect multiple host pathways, including HIF-1 signaling. Network pharmacology studies suggest that quercetin may inhibit the damage caused by HTNV infection in the host by regulating the host interaction genes and related pathways associated with HTNV. Combined transcriptomic and database analyses further suggested that quercetin may modulate apoptosis through targets including AKT1, BCL2, and STAT3. In baseline pharmacological assays in uninfected HEK293T cells, quercetin showed low cytotoxicity between 3.90625 and 7.8125 μM, increased cell viability, and reduced transcription of BCL2, MAPK3, and TNF. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding poses of quercetin within HTNV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), with Lys884 and Arg892 as predicted contact residues. In conclusion, these findings identify quercetin as a hypothesis-generating computational candidate for modulating HTNV-related host responses, pending experimental validation. This research framework can provide mechanistic hypotheses regarding host–pathogen interactions and potential intervention targets, thereby supporting the prevention and control of HTNV within the “One Health” framework.

papers.title: Integrated immunoinformatics and molecular dynamics approaches reveal a promising multi-epitope vaccine against hantavirus.
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Hantavirus is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen causing Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS), with substantial global morbidity and mortality. No universally approved human vaccine exists, making a safe, effective vaccine a public health priority. An immunoinformatics strategy was used to design a multi-epitope vaccine construct (MEVC) targeting the glycoprotein precursor (GP_HANTL) of Hantaan orthohantavirus. Cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL), helper T lymphocyte (HTL), and B-cell epitopes were predicted and screened for antigenicity, immunogenicity, MHC-binding affinity, and population coverage. Selected epitopes were joined with EAAAK, AAY, GPGPG, and KK linkers and fused to a β-defensin adjuvant. The construct was evaluated by physicochemical characterization, structural modeling, molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, immune simulation, codon optimization, and in silico cloning. The final construct comprised 10 CTL, 10 HTL, and 5 B-cell epitopes, with 99.24% global population coverage. Structural validation showed 95% of residues in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 82. Molecular docking produced a favorable ClusPro score (- 1273.6) for the selected MEVC-TLR4 complex. Immune simulations predicted robust humoral and cellular responses, including elevated antibodies, memory B cells, and CTL/HTL activation. Codon optimization yielded a CAI of 0.94, supporting efficient Escherichia coli expression. A 100-ns MD simulation showed substantial conformational adaptation of the MEVC while TLR4 remained comparatively stable; accompanying Rg and SASA trends indicated that the MEVC adopted a more compact state during the trajectory. The proposed MEVC demonstrated favorable predicted immunogenicity, favorable structural characteristics, broad population coverage, and favorable expression characteristics. These findings support experimental validation and development of a preventive strategy against Hantavirus infection. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40203-026-00782-6.

analysis.background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogen causing Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome, with substantial global morbidity and mortality (A1). No universally approved human vaccine exists, making vaccine development a public‑health priority (A2).
analysis.methods: An immunoinformatics strategy designed a multi‑epitope vaccine construct (MEVC) targeting the glycoprotein precursor of Hantaan orthohantavirus (A3). CTL, HTL, and B‑cell epitopes were predicted and screened for antigenicity, immunogenicity, MHC‑binding affinity, and population coverage (A4). Selected epitopes were joined with EAAAK, AAY, GPGPG, and KK linkers and fused to a β‑defensin adjuvant (A5). The construct underwent physicochemical characterization, structural modeling, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, immune simulation, codon optimization, and in silico cloning (A6).
analysis.results: The final construct comprised 10 CTL, 10 HTL, and 5 B‑cell epitopes with 99.24 % global population coverage (A7). Structural validation showed 95 % residues in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 82 (A8). Docking to TLR4 yielded a favorable ClusPro score of –1273.6 (A9). Immune simulations predicted robust humoral and cellular responses (A10). Codon optimization gave a CAI of 0.94 for E. coli expression (A11). A 100‑ns MD simulation indicated the MEVC adopted a more compact state while TLR4 remained stable, with supporting Rg and SASA trends (A12, A13).
analysis.contribution: The MEVC demonstrated favorable predicted immunogenicity, structural quality, broad population coverage, and expression characteristics, supporting experimental validation and development of a preventive strategy against hantavirus infection (A14, A15).
analysis.limitations: Only abstract‑level, computational results are presented; no experimental or in‑vivo validation is reported (abstract only).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus causes severe disease and lacks an approved human vaccine, creating a public‑health need (A1, A2). Methods: An immunoinformatics pipeline designed a multi‑epitope vaccine targeting the Hantaan glycoprotein, predicting CTL, HTL, and B‑cell epitopes, linking them with specific linkers and a β‑defensin adjuvant, and evaluating the construct via physicochemical, structural, docking, MD, immune simulation, and codon‑optimization analyses (A3‑A6). Results: The construct includes 10 CTL, 10 HTL, and 5 B‑cell epitopes covering 99.24 % of the global population; 95 % residues are in favored Ramachandran regions (ERRAT 82); docking to TLR4 gave a ClusPro score of –1273.6; immune simulation predicts strong humoral and cellular responses; codon optimization yields CAI 0.94; 100‑ns MD shows the vaccine becoming more compact while TLR4 stays stable (A7‑A13). Contribution: In silico data suggest the vaccine is immunogenic, structurally sound, broadly applicable, and expressible, supporting further experimental work (A14, A15). Limitations: Only abstract‑level computational findings are provided; no experimental validation is reported.

papers.title_zh: 综合免疫信息学与分子动力学方法揭示针对 汉坦病毒 的有前景的多表位疫苗。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 是一种啮齿动物传播的动物源性病原体,可导致 肾综合征出血热 和 汉坦病毒肺综合征,在全球范围内造成显著的发病率和死亡率 (A1)。目前尚无普遍获批的人用疫苗,使疫苗研发成为公共卫生的重点任务 (A2)。
analysis_zh.methods: 采用免疫信息学策略设计了针对Hantaan 正汉坦病毒 糖蛋白前体的多表位疫苗构建体(MEVC)(A3)。预测并筛选了CTL、HTL和B细胞表位,评估其抗原性、免疫原性、MHC结合亲和力及人群覆盖率 (A4)。选定的表位通过EAAAK、AAY、GPGPG和KK连接子连接,并与β-防御素佐剂融合 (A5)。该构建体随后进行理化特性分析、结构建模、分子对接、分子动力学模拟、免疫模拟、密码子优化及体外克隆 (A6)。
analysis_zh.contribution: MEVC显示出良好的预测免疫原性、结构质量、广泛的人群覆盖率和表达特性,为实验验证及针对 汉坦病毒 感染的预防策略开发提供支持 (A14, A15)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要层面的计算结果;未报告实验或体内验证(仅限摘要)。

papers.title: ArHa: A globally standardised, relational database of arenavirus and hantavirus sampling in wild small mammal populations
papers.abstract: Arenaviruses and hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens primarily hosted by small mammals. Efforts to map their ecological drivers and predict spillover risk are hindered by the fragmentation of historical surveillance data across the primary literature, compounded by shifting host nomenclature and variable geographic precision. We present ArHa, a database of 123,101 host occurrence and pathogen diagnostic records derived from a systematic review of published wild small mammal sampling. The dataset standardises host and pathogen taxonomies, resolves records of the same animals published in more than one paper, and classifies the spatial resolution and reliability of each coordinate to support bias-aware spatial epidemiology. To accurately preserve complex study designs, such as multiple diagnostic assays or genetic sequences derived from a single host, ArHa is structured as a four-tier relational database. This architecture handles many-to-one relationships and supports linkage without data duplication. The dataset is distributed as compressed Apache Parquet files for programmatic analysis and as a Darwin Core Archive, so that it can be read by standard biodiversity data tools. An accompanying interactive web application, the ArHa Database Explorer, allows users to filter, visualise, and export subsets of the database without requiring programming expertise. All data, extraction scripts, and the interactive web application are openly accessible via a permanent Zenodo repository.

papers.full_text: ArHa: A globally standardised, relational database of arenavirus and hantavirus sampling in wild small mammal populations David Simons1, Ricardo Rivero2, Grant Rickard2, Ana Martinez-Checa3, Harry Gordon4, Gregory C. Milne3, David W. Redding3, Stephanie N. Seifert2 1 Department of Anthropology, Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania, USA 2 Paul G. Allen School of Global Health, Washington State University, Pullman, Washington, USA 3 Science Department, Natural History Museum, London, UK 4 School of Biological Sciences, University of East Anglia, Norwich, UK Corresponding Authors: David Simons (dzs6259@psu.edu) and Stephanie N. Seifert (stephanie.seifert@wsu.edu) 1. Abstract Arenaviruses and hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens primarily hosted by small mammals. Efforts to map their ecological drivers and predict spillover risk are hindered by the fragmentation of historical surveillance data across the primary literature, compounded by shifting host nomenclature and variable geographic precision. We present ArHa, a database of 123,101 host occurrence and pathogen diagnostic records derived from a systematic review of published wild small mammal sampling. The dataset standardises host and pathogen taxonomies, resolves records of the same animals published in more than one paper, and classifies the spatial resolution and reliability of each coordinate to support bias-aware spatial epidemiology. To accurately preserve complex study designs, such as multiple diagnostic assays or genetic sequences derived from a single host, ArHa is structured as a four-tier relational database. This architecture handles many-to-one relationships and supports linkage without data duplication. The dataset is distributed as compressed Apache Parquet files for programmatic analysis and as a Darwin Core Archive, so that it can be read by standard biodiversity data tools. An accompanying interactive web application, the ArHa Database Explorer, allows users to filter, visualise, and export subsets of the database without requiring programming expertise. All data, extraction scripts, and the interactive web application are openly accessible via a permanent Zenodo repository. 1.1 Keywords Hantaviridae; Arenaviridae; rodent-borne zoonoses; wildlife disease surveillance; systematic review; relational database; spatial epidemiology; Darwin Core 2. Background & Summary Arenaviruses and hantaviruses represent substantial global zoonotic threats, primarily circulating within small mammal reservoirs of the orders Rodentia and Eulipotyphla (Jonsson et al. 2010; Childs and Peters 1993). The frequency and geographic extent of zoonotic spillover are driven by complex interactions between climate, land-use change, and host community ecology (Keesing et al. 2010; Yanagihara et al. 2014; McMahon et al. 2018). Predictive spillover modelling and spatial epidemiology depend on robust, broad- scale ecological data to parameterise these environmental drivers (Kreuder Johnson et al. 2015; Olival et al. 2017; Gibb, Albery, Becker, et al. 2021). However, the historical surveillance data required for such analyses remain highly fragmented across decades of isolated primary literature. This fragmentation restricts the ability to construct the global datasets required for macro-ecological modelling. Compounding this fragmentation is the challenge of harmonising historical ecological data through shifting taxonomic nomenclature and inconsistent spatial reporting. Reservoir host taxonomy has undergone substantial revision over the past half-century (Kryštufek et al. 2020). Without standardisation, these taxonomic shifts can artificially separate historical ecological baselines from contemporary genomic surveillance. Further, trapping data frequently lacks high-resolution geographic coordinates, often reporting sampling locations at the provincial or district level. Treating these aggregate, district-level reports as point-level occurrence data in spatial models risks introducing analytical bias by misaligning host occurrences with high-resolution environmental covariates (Lachish and Murray 2018; Gibb, Albery, Becker, et al. 2021). The ArHa database bridges raw historical field trapping data and modern analytical pipelines. By systematically extracting, standardising, and centralising published small mammal sampling data, ArHa addresses the barriers posed by shifting host nomenclature and inconsistent spatial and temporal reporting. Each record is annotated with a categorical geographic coordinate resolution (from trapping site, village, town, city or study area, through the third, second and first administrative levels, to country) and a categorical temporal resolution (from a full date, through day, month and year ranges, to dates inferred from the publication), alongside the taxonomic resolution of the sampled animal, allowing users to filter or weight records according to the precision required. ArHa uses a relational database structure to capture the complexity of historical study designs: where single specimens yield multiple diagnostic assay results or genetic sequences, this structure preserves those relationships without the record duplication inherent to flat-file formats, providing a robust, FAIR-compliant foundation for future research. 3. Methods 3.1 Literature Search and Data Extraction Searches of NCBI PubMed and Clarivate Web of Science on 16 October 2023 returned 4,020 records; with 11 records identified by other means, 2,755 unique records remained after de-duplication (Simons et al. 2025). Briefly, the extraction process captured study design, raw trapping effort (e.g., total trap nights), diagnostic assay methodologies, and NCBI GenBank accession numbers linking host and pathogen sequences. To preserve data provenance, the verbatim text from the primary literature was extracted before any harmonisation was applied. Data were extracted into the template set out in the protocol, with linked sheets for studies, small mammal sampling, pathogen assays and sequences (Simons et al. 2025). Of the 728 papers from which data were extracted, 26 were extracted by two team members. D.S. compared the two extractions of each of these papers and kept the more complete one; the choice is recorded in the processing scripts, and the other extraction is not part of the release. In a deviation from the registered protocol, AI tools (Claude Code, Opus 5.5, Anthropic) were used prior to finalisation of database: to find candidate cases of the same field data published in more than one paper, to check extracted records against their source papers and propose corrections, and to check coordinates that fell outside their stated country against the source papers. D.S. decided every cross-study duplicate action and every coordinate that was kept outside its stated country. The individual field corrections were not all reviewed by the authors; their accuracy was estimated from a random sample (see Technical Validation). The release also departs from the protocol in three other ways. The protocol planned to impute non-detections for species detected elsewhere in a study; this was not done, and non-detection records come only from what the papers report, recorded at extraction (see Trapping Effort). The protocol planned to give the uncertainty of each coordinate as a radius; the release gives a categorical coordinate resolution instead (see Technical Validation). Finally, the protocol planned to re-run the search once extraction was complete; it has not been re-run for this release (see Limitations). 3.2 Data Processing and Harmonisation Pipeline To transform the fragmented, verbatim extractions into a relational, machine-readable database, a sequential programmatic pipeline was developed in R (R Core Team 2023). This ensures reproducibility from raw data ingestion to the final database release. The pipeline comprises seven sequential phases: 3.2.1 Corrections to Extracted Records The extraction sheets are not edited after extraction. Corrections are listed in tables in the repository, each with its source in the paper: 3,243 corrections to individual values, 331 deleted rows and 316 re-extracted rows. The pipeline downloads the sheets and applies the corrections to the downloaded copy. It stops if a value in a sheet no longer matches the value a correction expects, so a correction cannot silently overwrite a later change. 3.2.2 Metadata Consolidation Raw extractions are aggregated to consolidate citation metadata and establish unique identifiers for all studies, hosts, pathogens, and sequences. Because historical literature reports temporal data in highly variable formats (e.g., specific days, month-year, multi-year spans), a parsing function was developed to translate verbatim event dates into standardised start_date and end_date bounds, generating a consistent temporal_resolution flag for every record. 3.2.3 Taxonomic and Spatial Resolution Host taxonomy is resolved via the taxize package (Chamberlain et al. 2020), querying the GBIF API to append standardised hierarchies (Species through Class) and persistent taxonID keys (Chamberlain et al. 2026). Concurrently, geographical point data undergo validation against standard administrative boundaries. Coordinates are matched to their corresponding ISO-3166 country codes, and a spatial join against the Database of Global Administrative Areas (GADM, version 4.1) enriches each record with standardised sub- national administrative levels (adm1, adm2, adm3) relevant to the level of geographic resolution (Database of Global Administrative Areas 2022; Hijmans et al. 2024). Where a paper gave no coordinates, the named locality (a village, town or administrative unit) was located using Google Maps, Wikipedia, OpenStreetMap or the GEOnet Names Server, and coordinate_resolution_processed records the level of that locality. One study gives its sites only as GADM version 2.8 municipality identifiers (Wang et al. 2023); these records are placed at a point inside each municipality. 3.2.4 Trapping Effort To support downstream macro-ecological modelling, unstructured, free-text trapping descriptions are parsed to extract trap-night metrics, recorded in trap_nights_clean and described by trap_nights_status. Where source manuscripts reported data in tabular form listing multiple species and sampling sites, zero-detection records were extracted directly from blank or absent cells, preserving the structure of the original study design. Users should be aware that a zero-detection record in host_occurrences reflects a recorded absence within a specific sample, and should not be interpreted as ecological absence from the broader study area. 3.2.5 Pathogen and Genomic Enrichment Pathogen nomenclature undergoes parallel harmonisation against the NCBI Taxonomy database (Schoch et al. 2020). To bridge the gap between ecological sampling and molecular epidemiology, raw NCBI GenBank accession numbers extracted from the literature are passed back through the NCBI Entrez API (Sayers et al. 2024). This automated sequence enrichment downloads and parses the metadata for each accession. The host and pathogen names in each GenBank record are then compared with the names assigned in ArHa, and the differences are listed in the quality assurance report. Differences are not corrected automatically, because GenBank host metadata are often incomplete or give a synonym, an older name or a higher taxon (see Technical Validation). 3.2.6 Cross-study Duplicate Resolution Some field data were published in more than one paper and so entered ArHa more than once. After enrichment, the pipeline resolves these cases from a table of decisions in the processing scripts. Records are removed where a paper repeats data already extracted from another, merged where two papers report complementary results for the same animals, and linked as a duplicate group where the same animals are reported at different spatial or temporal breakdowns that cannot be reconciled (duplicate_group and duplicate_role in sampling_events). How the duplicates were found, and how many, is described below. 3.2.7 Quality Assurance and Schema Formatting Prior to final compilation, the pipeline generates a quality assurance report to evaluate database dimensions, coordinate validity, and taxonomic consistency. The final output is then structured into the four-tier relational schema. 3.3 Duplicate Publication of Field Data The same field data may be published more than once: a survey reported in several papers, a synthesis that consolidates earlier studies, or results reanalysed in a later paper. Where a paper does not say that its data have been published before, extraction can duplicate data. The same animals, sites and assay results then enter the database more than once, affecting subsequent counts, prevalences and ranges drawn from, in ways that cannot be seen in the data. To find such cases, each assay record was given a fingerprint of host species, pathogen, number positive, number tested and country, and pairs of studies that shared these fingerprints with overlapping sampling dates were flagged; study totals were compared in the same way. Each flagged pair was checked against both papers. Of the 44 pairs checked, 19 shared counts by chance. The rest were resolved by pre-defined rules: keep the most complete source data; where two papers report the same animals at breakdowns that cannot be merged, keep both and link them; and do not treat a review, or a second copy of the same paper, as a source. In all, 15 studies were removed entirely. Of these, 5 were one paper entered under two citation records. A further 124 host records were removed where two papers overlapped in part, and 43 host records were merged where two papers reported different assays on the same animals. Studies reporting the same animals in formats that cannot be merged are retained and linked through duplicate_group and duplicate_role in sampling_events: 6 studies in 3 groups (see Usage Notes). Each action is listed in the processing scripts and summarised in duplicate_resolution.csv. 3.4 The ArHa Database Explorer To visualise the relational data architecture and improve accessibility for the wider ecological and public health communities, the database is accompanied by the ArHa Database Explorer (https://diddrog11.shinyapps.io/arenavirus_hantavirus_app/). Built using R and Shiny (Chang et al. 2025), with a DuckDB backend (Mühleisen and Raasveldt 2025) for relational querying and Leaflet/plotly for interactive spatial and statistical visualisation (Cheng et al. 2024; Sievert 2020). Users can spatially visualise genomic sampling via the Leaflet integration, cross-filter by diagnostic modality or host taxonomy, and export subsets of the data for local modelling. 3.5 Data Records The ArHa database is released under a dual-format strategy to maximise utility and interoperability. This release holds 710 studies with sampling in 103 countries at 4,910 distinct localities (Figure 1). Sampling began between 1964 and 2021 (Figure 2). Figure 1: Sampling localities in ArHa, coloured by the resolution of the reported location. Each point is a distinct coordinate; a coordinate used at more than one resolution is shown at its most precise. The numbers in the legend are localities. Figure 2: Contents of ArHa. (a) Studies by the year in which sampling began, for the 689 of 710 studies that report a sampling date. (b) Host records by order. (c) Assay records for Arenaviridae and Hantaviridae by assay type; “Other or not reported” includes virus culture, sequencing, Western blot and pooled serology or PCR. 106 assay records for other or unrecorded virus families are not shown. Host occurrence records tend not to be individual animals. Each record gives the number of animals of one taxon recorded in one sampling session at one locality, and 14,333 records (26.3%) record that a taxon was not caught (individualCount = 0). Records are also unevenly spread across studies: the three studies with the most records, two long- term population studies and one survey of many localities, hold 52% of host_occurrences (Mariën et al. 2020; Cuypers et al. 2023; Guzzetta et al. 2017). Cuypers et al. (2023), for example, sampled 187 localities in Tanzania and reported results for 54 small mammal taxa at each, contributing 10,120 records (18.6% of host_occurrences) from 1,224 animals. Most of these records document that a taxon was not caught at a locality rather than a capture. Analyses that treat records as equivalent units, without reference to individualCount, will therefore over-weight studies of this kind relative to those that report only captures. 3.5.1 Schema Definition A primary vulnerability when archiving complex ecological sampling in flat-file formats is data expansion: forcing many-to-many relationships (e.g., multiple diagnostic assays or genetic sequences derived from a single host) into a single two-dimensional table can result in substantial record duplication. To mitigate this and ensure data integrity, the ArHa dataset is engineered as a four-tier relational database, summarised in Table 1 and Figure 3. Figure 3: The four relational tables of ArHa, their roles in the Darwin Core Archive, their keys and the number of records. Arrows run from the referenced table to the table that holds the key. Assay records link to a sampling event and, where the paper allows, to a host record; sequence records link to either a host or an assay record. Table 1: Summary of the four ArHa relational tables. full_text_sections.full_text: ArHa: A globally standardised, relational database of arenavirus and hantavirus sampling in wild small mammal populations David Simons1, Ricardo Rivero2, Grant Rickard2, Ana Martinez-Checa3, Harry Gordon4, Gregory C. Milne3, David W. Redding3, Stephanie N. Seifert2 1 Department of Anthropology, Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania, USA 2 Paul G. Allen School of Global Health, Washington State University, Pullman, Washington, USA 3 Science Department, Natural History Museum, London, UK 4 School of Biological Sciences, University of East Anglia, Norwich, UK Corresponding Authors: David Simons (dzs6259@psu.edu) and Stephanie N. Seifert (stephanie.seifert@wsu.edu) 1. Abstract Arenaviruses and hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens primarily hosted by small mammals. Efforts to map their ecological drivers and predict spillover risk are hindered by the fragmentation of historical surveillance data across the primary literature, compounded by shifting host nomenclature and variable geographic precision. We present ArHa, a database of 123,101 host occurrence and pathogen diagnostic records derived from a systematic review of published wild small mammal sampling. The dataset standardises host and pathogen taxonomies, resolves records of the same animals published in more than one paper, and classifies the spatial resolution and reliability of each coordinate to support bias-aware spatial epidemiology. To accurately preserve complex study designs, such as multiple diagnostic assays or genetic sequences derived from a single host, ArHa is structured as a four-tier relational database. This architecture handles many-to-one relationships and supports linkage without data duplication. The dataset is distributed as compressed Apache Parquet files for programmatic analysis and as a Darwin Core Archive, so that it can be read by standard biodiversity data tools. An accompanying interactive web application, the ArHa Database Explorer, allows users to filter, visualise, and export subsets of the database without requiring programming expertise. All data, extraction scripts, and the interactive web application are openly accessible via a permanent Zenodo repository. 1.1 Keywords Hantaviridae; Arenaviridae; rodent-borne zoonoses; wildlife disease surveillance; systematic review; relational database; spatial epidemiology; Darwin Core 2. Background & Summary Arenaviruses and hantaviruses represent substantial global zoonotic threats, primarily circulating within small mammal reservoirs of the orders Rodentia and Eulipotyphla (Jonsson et al. 2010; Childs and Peters 1993). The frequency and geographic extent of zoonotic spillover are driven by complex interactions between climate, land-use change, and host community ecology (Keesing et al. 2010; Yanagihara et al. 2014; McMahon et al. 2018). Predictive spillover modelling and spatial epidemiology depend on robust, broad- scale ecological data to parameterise these environmental drivers (Kreuder Johnson et al. 2015; Olival et al. 2017; Gibb, Albery, Becker, et al. 2021). However, the historical surveillance data required for such analyses remain highly fragmented across decades of isolated primary literature. This fragmentation restricts the ability to construct the global datasets required for macro-ecological modelling. Compounding this fragmentation is the challenge of harmonising historical ecological data through shifting taxonomic nomenclature and inconsistent spatial reporting. Reservoir host taxonomy has undergone substantial revision over the past half-century (Kryštufek et al. 2020). Without standardisation, these taxonomic shifts can artificially separate historical ecological baselines from contemporary genomic surveillance. Further, trapping data frequently lacks high-resolution geographic coordinates, often reporting sampling locations at the provincial or district level. Treating these aggregate, district-level reports as point-level occurrence data in spatial models risks introducing analytical bias by misaligning host occurrences with high-resolution environmental covariates (Lachish and Murray 2018; Gibb, Albery, Becker, et al. 2021). The ArHa database bridges raw historical field trapping data and modern analytical pipelines. By systematically extracting, standardising, and centralising published small mammal sampling data, ArHa addresses the barriers posed by shifting host nomenclature and inconsistent spatial and temporal reporting. Each record is annotated with a categorical geographic coordinate resolution (from trapping site, village, town, city or study area, through the third, second and first administrative levels, to country) and a categorical temporal resolution (from a full date, through day, month and year ranges, to dates inferred from the publication), alongside the taxonomic resolution of the sampled animal, allowing users to filter or weight records according to the precision required. ArHa uses a relational database structure to capture the complexity of historical study designs: where single specimens yield multiple diagnostic assay results or genetic sequences, this structure preserves those relationships without the record duplication inherent to flat-file formats, providing a robust, FAIR-compliant foundation for future research. 3. Methods 3.1 Literature Search and Data Extraction Searches of NCBI PubMed and Clarivate Web of Science on 16 October 2023 returned 4,020 records; with 11 records identified by other means, 2,755 unique records remained after de-duplication (Simons et al. 2025). Briefly, the extraction process captured study design, raw trapping effort (e.g., total trap nights), diagnostic assay methodologies, and NCBI GenBank accession numbers linking host and pathogen sequences. To preserve data provenance, the verbatim text from the primary literature was extracted before any harmonisation was applied. Data were extracted into the template set out in the protocol, with linked sheets for studies, small mammal sampling, pathogen assays and sequences (Simons et al. 2025). Of the 728 papers from which data were extracted, 26 were extracted by two team members. D.S. compared the two extractions of each of these papers and kept the more complete one; the choice is recorded in the processing scripts, and the other extraction is not part of the release. In a deviation from the registered protocol, AI tools (Claude Code, Opus 5.5, Anthropic) were used prior to finalisation of database: to find candidate cases of the same field data published in more than one paper, to check extracted records against their source papers and propose corrections, and to check coordinates that fell outside their stated country against the source papers. D.S. decided every cross-study duplicate action and every coordinate that was kept outside its stated country. The individual field corrections were not all reviewed by the authors; their accuracy was estimated from a random sample (see Technical Validation). The release also departs from the protocol in three other ways. The protocol planned to impute non-detections for species detected elsewhere in a study; this was not done, and non-detection records come only from what the papers report, recorded at extraction (see Trapping Effort). The protocol planned to give the uncertainty of each coordinate as a radius; the release gives a categorical coordinate resolution instead (see Technical Validation). Finally, the protocol planned to re-run the search once extraction was complete; it has not been re-run for this release (see Limitations). 3.2 Data Processing and Harmonisation Pipeline To transform the fragmented, verbatim extractions into a relational, machine-readable database, a sequential programmatic pipeline was developed in R (R Core Team 2023). This ensures reproducibility from raw data ingestion to the final database release. The pipeline comprises seven sequential phases: 3.2.1 Corrections to Extracted R…

papers.title: Rational Design of Candidate Hantavirus Gc Fusion Inhibitors Through Structure-Activity Relationship Analysis
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, for which no targeted antiviral therapy exists. The viral glycoprotein Gc drives host cell entry through an effectively irreversible prefusion to postfusion transition, making the prefusion state a target for small molecule stabilization. A binding site was defined by comparing the prefusion (PDB 5LJY) and postfusion (PDB 5LJZ) conformations. Residues 308-320 undergo a non-uniform transition: the segments 308-311 and 318-320 preserved their internal geometry (span changes +0.4 Å and + 0.7 Å) while the central segment contracted sharply (313-317: 11.9 -> 6.1 Å). The selected pocket, bounded by Pro46, Lys310, Asp311, Ile312 and Phe314 therefore spans a rigid anchoring region and an adjacent deformation zone. A library of approximately three million compounds was reduced to 1,041 docking-ready ligands and docked against prefusion Gc (mean predicted affinity -5.35 kcal/mol). Two parent scaffolds (compounds 512 and 74) were carried into 38 analogues (SAR-v1-v20; MR-v1-v18) across a four node decomposition of the pocket. Each was redocked 10 times and assessed by DBSCAN pose clustering, a Gaussian residue contact fingerprint, an ensemble pose-drift index, and MM/GBSA rescoring after a short time scale relaxation (2 failed to parameterize). No significant pairwise correlations were detected among the three ranking criteria (residue-contact score versus MM/GBSA, Spearman ρ = 0.09, p = 0.59), so none was treated as decisive. SAR-v17 ranked first of 38 by weighted residue-contact score, ninth of 36 by MM/GBSA (-11.08 kcal/mol) and fifteenth of 38 by ensemble drift (0.094 Å), all ten poses fell within a single DBSCAN cluster. It was the analouge with the best mean rank among the SAR and MR series. SAR-v20 was retained as a comparator because it only differed in structure to SAR-v17 by a single atom. All findings are predictions; no binding, fusion-inhibition or antiviral assay has been performed.

source_records.title: Rational Design of Candidate Hantavirus Gc Fusion Inhibitors Through Structure-Activity Relationship Analysis
source_records.abstract: Hantaviruses cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, for which no targeted antiviral therapy exists. The viral glycoprotein Gc drives host cell entry through an effectively irreversible prefusion to postfusion transition, making the prefusion state a target for small molecule stabilization. A binding site was defined by comparing the prefusion (PDB 5LJY) and postfusion (PDB 5LJZ) conformations. Residues 308-320 undergo a non-uniform transition: the segments 308-311 and 318-320 preserved their internal geometry (span changes +0.4 Å and + 0.7 Å) while the central segment contracted sharply (313-317: 11.9 -> 6.1 Å). The selected pocket, bounded by Pro46, Lys310, Asp311, Ile312 and Phe314 therefore spans a rigid anchoring region and an adjacent deformation zone. A library of approximately three million compounds was reduced to 1,041 docking-ready ligands and docked against prefusion Gc (mean predicted affinity -5.35 kcal/mol). Two parent scaffolds (compounds 512 and 74) were carried into 38 analogues (SAR-v1-v20; MR-v1-v18) across a four node decomposition of the pocket. Each was redocked 10 times and assessed by DBSCAN pose clustering, a Gaussian residue contact fingerprint, an ensemble pose-drift index, and MM/GBSA rescoring after a short time scale relaxation (2 failed to parameterize). No significant pairwise correlations were detected among the three ranking criteria (residue-contact score versus MM/GBSA, Spearman ρ = 0.09, p = 0.59), so none was treated as decisive. SAR-v17 ranked first of 38 by weighted residue-contact score, ninth of 36 by MM/GBSA (-11.08 kcal/mol) and fifteenth of 38 by ensemble drift (0.094 Å), all ten poses fell within a single DBSCAN cluster. It was the analouge with the best mean rank among the SAR and MR series. SAR-v20 was retained as a comparator because it only differed in structure to SAR-v17 by a single atom. All findings are predictions; no binding, fusion-inhibition or antiviral assay has been performed.

papers.title: Diagnostic Preparedness and Biosafety Measures for Hantavirus Infections in Clinical Laboratories: A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Background: Hantavirus infections are potentially severe zoonotic diseases whose effective laboratory management requires timely clinical recognition, reliable diagnostic testing, appropriate biosafety practices, and surveillance of animal reservoirs. In the Philippines, evidence of human exposure and hantavirus circulation in wildlife exists, but contemporary information on hantavirus-specific diagnostic and biosafety preparedness remains limited. Methods: This systematic review evaluated evidence on hantavirus epidemiology, clinical recognition, laboratory diagnosis, reservoir surveillance, occupational exposure, and biosafety, with particular emphasis on implications for Philippine clinical laboratories. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and supplementary sources were searched. Of 304 records initially identified, 18 studies met the eligibility criteria. Because of substantial heterogeneity in study designs, populations, diagnostic approaches, and outcomes, findings were synthesized narratively and thematically. Results: Philippine evidence demonstrated 6.1% hantavirus antibody prevalence among 461 asymptomatic participants and molecular detection of Quezon virus in local wildlife. International studies demonstrated that hantavirus infection may be clinically misrecognized, including as dengue, and severe HPS was associated with substantial mortality. Molecular diagnostic studies showed that RT-qPCR can facilitate early detection, with one study reporting 94.9% sensitivity and 100% specificity. Serological and molecular methods were complementary, while reservoir studies demonstrated considerable hantavirus diversity. Occupational investigations documented laboratory-associated infections and highlighted aerosol exposure, infected animals, and potentially infectious specimens as important biosafety risks. Philippine studies demonstrated existing biosafety training capacity but identified broader gaps in biorisk management and pathogen-specific preparedness. Conclusion: Evidence of human exposure and wildlife-associated hantavirus circulation supports strengthened preparedness in the Philippines. A risk-based, tiered, and One Health approach integrating clinical recognition, serological and molecular testing, specimen-referral systems, quality assurance, biosafety training, occupational protection, and human–animal surveillance is warranted. Contemporary Philippine studies are needed to define current exposure, circulating viruses, and laboratory readiness.

INTRODUCTION Hantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses of the family Hantaviridae that are maintained primarily in rodent and other small-mammal reservoirs and transmitted to humans mainly through inhalation of aerosolized virus-contaminated urine, feces, or saliva [1]. Medically important hantaviruses cause two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), occurring predominantly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) or hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), reported mainly in the Americas [2, 3]. The potentially severe clinical course of these infections makes early laboratory recognition and appropriate biosafety practices essential [4]. Laboratory assessment of hantavirus infection relies principally on serological and molecular methods [5]. Detection of hantavirus-specific IgM and IgG antibodies using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) is widely employed, while reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) enables detection of viral RNA, particularly during the acute phase [2]. Immunofluorescence, immunoblotting, neutralization assays, and immunohistochemistry may provide supplementary or confirmatory evidence [6]. The effectiveness of hantavirus diagnosis depends not only on the analytical performance of serological and molecular assays but also on the broader laboratory system in which testing occurs [7]. Essential components include appropriate laboratory infrastructure, trained personnel, early recognition and notification of suspected cases, safe specimen collection and transport, functional referral pathways to authorized reference laboratories, and quality-assurance procedures that support reliable and timely results [8]. Diagnostic preparedness must therefore be accompanied by appropriate biosafety and biorisk-management measures to protect laboratory personnel, prevent laboratory-associated transmission, and ensure that testing can be performed safely and reliably [9]. Laboratory personnel may encounter potentially infectious clinical specimens before hantavirus infection is recognized, creating occupational risks from aerosol-generating procedures, accidental percutaneous inoculation, mucous-membrane exposure, and contamination of work surfaces [10]. Risk-based precautions include appropriate personal protective equipment, biological safety cabinets, safe centrifugation, specimen inactivation where appropriate, decontamination, waste management, exposure-response procedures, and higher containment for activities involving propagation or concentration of live virus [11]. These measures are particularly important in laboratories with limited experience handling uncommon or emerging zoonotic pathogens, where agent-specific training, documented risk assessment, competency verification, and access to expert or reference-laboratory support may be limited [9]. At the population level, hantavirus infection remains an important zoonotic and public-health concern, with transmission shaped by rodent abundance, occupational and recreational exposure, climatic variability, urbanization, agricultural activity, and environmental disturbance [12]. Agricultural and forestry workers, military personnel, wildlife handlers, sanitation workers, and laboratory personnel may experience increased occupational exposure to hantaviruses through activities that bring them into contact with infected rodents, their excreta, contaminated environments, or potentially infectious specimens [13]. A recent global review reported that hantavirus seroprevalence among several occupational populations exceeded background population levels, emphasizing the importance of integrated surveillance, prevention, and occupational protection [3, 14]. These findings demonstrate that laboratory preparedness forms part of a broader One Health response connecting human health, reservoir surveillance, and environmental risk. In the Philippines, hantavirus remains underrecognized despite ecological conditions favorable to rodent-borne zoonoses and historical evidence of human exposure. Earlier seroepidemiological research demonstrated hantavirus antibodies among Filipino populations [15]. Philippine evidence indicates that hantavirus exposure has occurred in human populations, while studies of rodents and other wildlife suggest possible viral circulation in animal reservoirs. However, the available evidence remains limited by geographically restricted studies, incomplete surveillance, insufficient characterization of occupational and environmental risk factors, and constrained diagnostic capacity [15, 16]. The review emphasized the need for strengthened One Health surveillance, improved diagnostic capability, ecological monitoring, and occupational biosafety [17]. Evidence from other Asian countries, Europe, and the Americas is nevertheless essential because established diagnostic and biosafety systems internationally may provide approaches that can be adapted to Philippine and other resource-limited laboratory settings [18]. Despite growing research on hantavirus epidemiology, reservoir ecology, occupational exposure, and diagnostic techniques, important gaps remain in the integration of clinical laboratory preparedness and biosafety within hantavirus response systems [12]. Current international guidance emphasizes that laboratory confirmation requires appropriate serological or molecular testing, while potentially infectious specimens must be handled, packaged, transported, and processed under risk-appropriate containment conditions [1]. However, preparedness also depends on trained personnel, quality-management systems, validated procedures, referral networks, and sufficient resources. A recent Asia-Pacific assessment involving substantial participation from Philippine laboratories identified staff-training and budget limitations among the major barriers to strengthening laboratory quality and competence, indicating broader system-level constraints that may also affect preparedness for uncommon emerging pathogens [19]. These limitations are particularly relevant to hantavirus preparedness in the Philippines. In June 2026, the Research Institute for Tropical Medicine issued specific instructions for the collection, handling, packaging, transport, and referral of specimens from suspected hantavirus cases, emphasizing personnel safety, specimen integrity, coordination with designated reference laboratories, and compliance with biosafety and biosecurity standards [18]. Nevertheless, the existence of national referral guidance does not necessarily indicate that hantavirus testing and biosafety procedures are routinely implemented across hospital and clinical laboratories. Thus, limited evidence regarding decentralized diagnostic capacity, laboratory personnel competency, quality assurance, containment practices, and functional referral pathways represents an important knowledge gap. Systematically evaluating these areas is necessary to determine how effectively Philippine laboratories could recognize suspected hantavirus infections and safely manage and refer to associated clinical specimens, while drawing lessons from laboratory systems in other countries. . Therefore, this systematic review aims to evaluate diagnostic preparedness and biosafety measures for hantavirus infections in clinical laboratories, with particular consideration of their applicability to the Philippines. Specifically, it seeks to identify and compare diagnostic methods used for hantavirus detection; assess laboratory preparedness, testing capacity, quality assurance, and specimen-referral systems; evaluate biosafety measures for specimen collection, processing, transport, storage, and disposal; compare practices across countries and resource settings; identify major diagnostic and biosafety gaps; and determine evidence-based strategies that may strengthen hantavirus laboratory preparedness in the Philippines and comparable resource-limited settings. METHODOLOGY 2.1Study Design and Reporting Framework This study employed a systematic review design to identify, evaluate, and synthesize available evidence on hantavirus infection, with particular attention to epidemiology, human exposure, clinical manifestations, laboratory diagnosis, reservoir surveillance, biosafety, and implications for public health and laboratory preparedness in the Philippines. The review was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement [20]. A structured approach was applied to literature identification, screening and eligibility assessment, data extraction, methodological appraisal, and evidence synthesis. The review protocol was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) [39] under registration number CRD420261485094. Given the heterogeneity of the included evidence in terms of study design, geographical setting, study populations, diagnostic approaches, exposure measures, and reported outcomes, a meta-analysis was not considered appropriate. Instead, findings were synthesized using a narrative and thematic approach, allowing evidence to be organized and interpreted across the major domains addressed by the review. 2.2 Literature Search Strategy A comprehensive literature search was conducted to identify studies relevant to hantavirus infection and its epidemiological, clinical, laboratory, ecological, and public health dimensions. The principal electronic databases searched were PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Supplementary searches were undertaken through manual screening of reference lists and relevant institutional and research repositories. Grey literature and technical documents from recognized public health organizations and national agencies were also considered when they contributed directly to the objectives of the review. Search terms were combined using Boolean operators and included terms related to Hantavirus, Orthohantavirus, human–rodent interaction, zoonotic transmission, occupational exposure, seroprevalence, reservoir surveillance, laboratory diagnosis, and public health. An example of the search strategy was: (Hantavirus or Orthohantavirus) and (occupational exposure or human–rodent interface or zoonotic transmission) and (seroprevalence or reservoir surveillance or public health) Search terms were modified where necessary to accommodate the indexing systems and search functions of individual databases. 2.3 Eligibility Criteria Studies were considered eligible when they provided evidence relevant to hantavirus infection or transmission, including human exposure, seroprevalence, clinical disease, laboratory diagnosis, occupational or environmental risk, rodent reservoirs, ecological or molecular surveillance, outbreaks, biosafety, or public health implications. Eligible evidence included observational studies such as cross-sectional, cohort, and case-control studies, as well as outbreak investigations, seroepidemiological studies, ecological and molecular surveillance studies, and other relevant primary investigations. Selected authoritative technical and public health documents were considered when they provided information directly relevant to laboratory diagnosis, surveillance, biosafety, or preparedness. Studies were excluded when they were unrelated to the objectives of the review, provided insufficient information for meaningful interpretation, represented duplicate publications, consisted primarily of opinion or editorial material, or could not provide adequate information for eligibility assessment. Duplicate records identified during the search and screening process were retained only once. 2.4 Study Selection and Screening All records retrieved from the literature search were compiled and screened systematically. The initial search identified 304 records. Duplicate records were removed before screening, after which titles and abstracts were evaluated against the predetermined eligibility criteria. Potentially relevant publications were subsequently assessed through full-text review. Studies that did not satisfy the eligibility criteria at the full-text stage were excluded, with the principal reasons for exclusion documented. Following completion of the screening and eligibility assessment, 18 studies met the inclusion criteria and were retained for the final systematic review.
