Our 75 framework offers a practical tool for hantavirus genomics and a foundation for 76 investigating how defective genomes shape hantavirus infection. 77 3 INTRODUCTION 78 Orthohantaviruses (family Hantaviridae, class Bunyaviricetes) are zoonotic segmented 79 negative-sense RNA viruses that are naturally found in small mammal species, 80 including rodents, shrews, moles and bats (1). Human infections occur primarily through 81 inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected animal hosts and can cause severe 82 disease, including haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and nephropathia 83 epidemica (NE) caused by Old World hantaviruses primarily in Eurasia and hantavirus 84 cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by New World hantaviruses in the Americas 85 (2, 3). Case fatality rates for hantavirus diseases vary significantly depending on the 86 infecting virus species (4): it ranges from <1% for Puumala virus (PUUV), the causative 87 agent for NE, to up to 15% for HFRS-causing Old World hantaviruses such as Hantaan 88 virus (HTNV) in East Asia and Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) in eastern Europe, and 89 over 30% for HCPS-causing New World hantaviruses such as Andes virus (ANDV) and 90 Sin Nombre virus (SNV). 91 Hantaviruses have small tripartite negative-sense RNA genomes comprising the small 92 (S), medium (M) and large (L) genome segments, encoding only 4-5 viral proteins (5). 93 The S segment encodes the nucleoprotein (NP) and in some cases a non-structural 94 (NS) protein, the M segment encodes the glycoprotein precursor (GPC) which is co- 95 translationally cleaved into the Gn and Gc glycoproteins, and the L segment encodes 96 the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The genetic sequence divergence at the 97 amino acid level is significant across the hantavirus family (up to 75%) and even within 98 a species (up to 24%) (6). Low viral RNA copy numbers in clinical and rodent samples, 99 and natural RNA degradation outside of infected hosts makes obtaining complete 100 coverage of hantavirus genomes challenging (7, 8). Current state-of-the-art sequencing 101 approaches include metagenome sequencing, tiled amplicon sequencing and hybrid 102 capture-based sequencing, which all require extensive optimisation and large numbers 103 of probes (9–12). Existing long-read amplicon-based sequencing approaches often 104 include single amplicons for the smaller segments, but to date, there are no established 105 protocols to reliably capture the entire L segment in a single amplicon. In addition, while 106 these methods can provide full genome coverage sequencing and provide consensus 107 sequences of viruses, they do not accurately reflect the genetic makeup of any given 108 virus population. In reality, virus populations are highly heterogeneous and contain large 109 proportions of defective viral genomes (DVGs) consisting of genome truncations, 110 duplications and recombinations (13). However, DVGs have so far never been reported 111 for hantaviruses. 112 Here, we designed a whole segment amplicon-based long-read nanopore sequencing 113 method and an end-to-end bioinformatical analysis pipeline for hantavirus genome 114 assembly, alignment, consensus sequence generation, variant calling and defective 115 viral genome analysis (Fig.1A). This approach minimises required optimisation steps for 116 tiling and hybridization probes and enables a much more accurate depiction of 117 heterogenous virus populations without sacrificing sensitivity or genome coverage. 118 Using this method, we were able to sequence several diverse PUUV strains from both 119 infected cell cultures and from bank voles – their natural host species. In addition, we 120 validated our method using representative members of the whole Orthohantavirus 121 genus and samples obtained from cell cultures and animal tissues. Our sequencing 122 4 approach provides a cost-effective and rapid end-to-end pipeline to analyse hantavirus 123 genomes from environmental, animal and cellular samples. In addition, we provide the 124 first report of hantavirus DVGs and provide a framework for their analysis. 125 126 127 RESULTS 128 A nanopore sequencing and bioinformatics pipeline. Here, we designed a 129 whole segment amplicon-based long-read nanopore sequencing method. Hantavirus 130 RNA is reverse transcribed using universal hantavirus primers that hybridize with the 131 highly conserved 14 nucleotides at the genome termini. Subsequently, each genome 132 segment is amplified in a virus species-specific manner using a single longer primer pair 133 corresponding to the specific genome termini of a virus genome segment. PCR 134 products are then sequenced using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read 135 sequencing technology. This is followed by a bioinformatical analysis pipeline that 136 includes hantavirus reference-guided genome assembly, genome alignment, consensus 137 sequence generation, variant calling and DVG analysis (Fig.1A). The DVG analysis is 138 performed using the ‘ONT-based Recombination and Copy-back Haplotype 139 Identification for DVGs’ (ORCHID) pipeline which detects recombination events in virus 140 genomes and classifies these as artefacts, deletion, or copy-back events (Fig. 1B). 141 Deletion DVGs (delVGs) are produced when the RdRp dissociates from the genome 142 template during replication, continues reading the template without copying any of it, 143 and then reassociates and starts copying the template further downstream, thus 144 creating an internal deletion of the copied genome (Fig. 1C). Copy-back DVGs (cbVGs) 145 are produced when the RdRp dissociates from the template strand during replication 146 and reengages the nascent product strand as a new template (Fig. 1C). Together, this 147 workflow represents a highly customisable end-to-end sequencing and analysis 148 framework for hantaviruses. 149 150 Establishment of whole hantavirus segment amplification. While amplification 151 of the S and M segments in single amplicons has been achieved before, capturing the 152 entire L segment in one single amplicon has so far proven difficult (10). We utilized the 153 extremely high sequence conservation in the terminal 14 nucleotides of the 5’ and 3’ 154 ends of all three genome segments across the entire Orthohantavirus genus to design 155 universal hantavirus reverse transcription primers for both genomic negative-sense viral 156 RNA (vRNA) and the antigenomic positive-sense complementary RNA (cRNA) (Fig. 157 2A). Primers for amplification of individual segments also contained these highly 158 conserved termini but stretched further into the segments to achieve high specificity for 159 virus species and segments. 160 We established and optimised our virus species- and segment-specific viral genome 161 segment RT-PCR (vgsRT-PCR) method on RNA extracted from a cell-free purified 162 PUUV stock. First, we compared different RT primers and found that the Uni-c14 163 primer, random hexamers and oligo(dT) primers performed poorly and resulted in low or 164 no detectable amplification of PUUV segments (Fig. 2B). This was an expected result, 165 since hantaviruses generally are not thought to contain polyadenylation signals and 166 since the virus stock primarily should be composed of vRNA (14, 15). However, use of 167 5 the vRNA-specific Uni-v14 primer alone or in combination with the cRNA-specific Uni- 168 c14 primer yielded strong full-length amplification of all three PUUV segments. 169 Henceforth, the combination of vRNA- and cRNA-specific RT primers was used. Next, 170 different PCR elongation times and cycle numbers were compared. We observed that 171 for the longer L and M segments, increasing elongation time seemed to slightly increase 172 full-length segment amplification, while no major difference was observed for the S 173 segment (Fig. 2C). Based on these data we selected an elongation time of 3 min as the 174 best balance between sensitivity and overall reaction time. Increasing PCR cycle 175 numbers steadily increased PCR product accumulation in all three segments, with 176 robust product accumulation starting at 30 cycles (Fig 2D). As a compromise between 177 sensitivity, PCR bias and time optimisation, we chose 30 cycles as our default option, 178 with the possibility of increasing cycles to 40 for samples that require higher sensitivity. 179 As a proof-of-concept we also tested whether all segment-specific primers can be 180 combined in a single reaction and confirmed that all PUUV segments were efficiently 181 and equally amplified compared to the single primer pair reactions (Fig. 2E). Sensitivity 182 is important when designing PCR protocols for hantaviruses due to their inherently low 183 RNA copy numbers in infected patients. Using in vitro transcribed PUUV S segment 184 vRNA as a standard, we were able to accurately detect up to 101 RNA copies by RT- 185 qPCR (Fig. 2F) and up to 103 RNA copies by vgsRT-PCR (Fig. 2G). 186 Overall, we established a reproducible and sensitive vgsRT-PCR method for the optimal 187 amplification of whole PUUV segments with a single primer pair per segment. 188 189 Nanopore sequencing of diverse PUUV strains from cell culture. Having 190 established that we can robustly amplify full-length PUUV genomes, we next attempted 191 to sequence and characterise these amplicons from more complex samples by ONT 192 long-read sequencing. To that end, we infected human lung epithelial cells with several 193 different PUUV strains and extracted RNA from infected cells. First, we confirmed and 194 compared the presence of viral RNA by RT-qPCR and found robust – but varying – 195 levels of viral RNA in all samples (Fig.3A). Analysis of vgsRT-PCR products by gel 196 electrophoresis demonstrated clean amplification of the full M and S segments for all 197 PUUV strains (Fig. 3B). However, for the L segment we predominantly observed PCR 198 products of varying shorter lengths, suggesting production of internally truncated DVGs 199 that maintained the conserved segment termini. This was especially pronounced for the 200 PUUV strain BE/Cg/Villers-la-Tour/1/2009 (‘Villers-la-Tour’), BE/Cg/Seloignes/1/2009 201 (‘Seloignes’), BE/Cg/Beaumont/1/2012 (‘Beaumont’), and BE/Cg/Turnhout/1/1985 202 (‘Turnhout’), while RUS/Cg/Kazan/E6/1982 (‘Kazan-E6’) exhibited relatively clean full- 203 length products. Interestingly, while these putative DVGs exhibited strain-specific 204 profiles, the overall size distribution appears similar across all virus strains. 205 Nanopore sequencing of these amplicons demonstrated high levels of sequencing 206 depth across the entire genome (Table 1 and Fig. 3C). The genome coverage was even 207 across the entire genome for the M and S segments for all PUUV strains, confirming our 208 previous vgsRT-PCR data. Accordingly, we observed a striking reduction in genome 209 coverage in the central regions of the L segment for all strains except Kazan-E6, which 210 also did not generate any major truncated PCR products. We used the ORCHID 211 pipeline to classify sequenced viral reads and confirmed our vgsRT-PCR and genome 212 6 coverage data: while the M and S segments only contained small fractions of putative 213 and high-confidence DVGs, the vast majority of L segment reads were classified as 214 delVGs (Table 1 and Fig. 3D). Only Kazan-E6 exhibited a lower – yet still significant – 215 fraction of DVGs, consistent with our previous findings. As the M and S segments did 216 not exhibit any meaningful levels of DVGs, and cbVGs could not be detected at 217 significant levels in any segment, we characterized only L segment delVGs further. 218 Analysis of L segment delVG junction sizes revealed a now familiar pattern: while 219 Kazan-E6 only showed few unique junctions that were concentrated between 3000 and 220 4000 nt in size, all the remaining strains almost exclusively had very large 221 (approximately 4000 to 6000 nt in size) deletions (Fig. 3E). This helps explain why we 222 previously observed a relatively uniform pattern of truncated PCR products (Fig. 3B). 223 Investigation of the exact junction sites – i.e. at what nucleotide position of the genome 224 the RdRp disengages from the template (junction start) and then subsequently 225 reengages again (junction end) – helps shed further light onto the nature of these DVGs 226 and reveals highly specific regions in the PUUV L segment that are associated with 227 delVG formation (Fig. 3F). For the Turnhout, Beaumont, Seloignes and Villers-la-Tour 228 strains we observed highly similar patterns: the majority of deletions start within the first 229 100 nt of the 5’ end of the L segment and span almost the entire segment and end 230 within a more variable (approximately 1500 nt) window at the 3’ end of the segment 231 (Fig.3F). 232 Together, these data demonstrated that our whole segment amplicon sequencing 233 method is able to robustly sequence and resolve entire PUUV genomes. In addition, our 234 analysis framework allows us to confidently call and characterise DVGs from nanopore 235 sequencing data, identifying high abundance delVGs in most PUUV L segments. 236 237 Sequencing of PUUV geno…

Twohig2, Anne Tuiskunen Bäck3,4,5,6, Magnus 5 Sjöblom7, Rebecca Lantto3, Gabriella Svala7, Janne Tynell8,9, Sandra Broddesson10,11, 6 Robert Dyrdak10,11, Wanda Christ1, Silke Riesle-Sbarbaro12, Joseph B. Prescott12, 7 Steven B. Bradfute2, Daniel P. Depledge13,14,15, Benjamin E. Nilsson-Payant1 8 9 1 Division of Virology and Immunology, Department of Microbiology, Tumor and Cell 10 Biology, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden 11 2 Department of Internal Medicine, Center for Global Health, University of New Mexico 12 Health Sciences Center, Albuquerque, New Mexico, United States of America 13 3 Department of Clinical Microbiology, Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden 14 4 Department of Public Health and Clinical Medicine, Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden 15 5 Umeå Centre for Microbial Research (UCMR), Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden 16 6 Laboratory for Molecular Infection Medicine Sweden (MIMS), Umeå University, Umeå, 17 Sweden 18 7 Clinical Microbiology Unit, Department of Laboratory Medicine, Sunderby Hospital, 19 Luleå, Sweden 20 8 Department of Virology, University of Helsinki, Helsinki, Finland 21 9 Institute of Biomedicine, University of Turku, Turku, Finland 22 10 Division of Clinical Genomics & Virology, Department of Microbiology, Tumor and Cell 23 Biology, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden 24 11 Department of Clinical Microbiology, Karolinska University Hospital, Stockholm, 25 Sweden 26 12 Center for Biological Threats and Special Pathogens, Robert Koch Institute, Berlin, 27 Germany 28 13 Institute of Virology, Hannover Medical School, Hannover, Germany 29 14 Cluster of Excellence RESIST (EXC 2155), Hannover Medical School, Hannover 30 Germany 31 15 German Center for Infection Research (DZIF), partner site Hannover-Braunschweig, 32 Hannover, Germany 33 34 35 Corresponding author: benjamin.nilssonpayant@ki.se 36 37 38 39 40 2 ABSTRACT 41 Orthohantaviruses are zoonotic, tri-segmented negative-sense RNA viruses of rodents 42 and other small mammals that can cause severe human disease. Whole genome 43 sequencing remains difficult because of low viral loads, high sequence diversity, and an 44 inherent instability of the viral L segment. Current tiled amplicon and hybrid-capture 45 approaches do not capture the heterogeneity of virus populations, including defective 46 viral genomes (DVGs), which have never been described for hantaviruses. Here, we 47 present an Oxford Nanopore Technologies sequencing framework based on universal 48 reverse transcription primers targeting the conserved genome termini of 49 orthohantaviruses and a single species-specific primer pair per segment, enabling 50 amplification and sequencing of complete S, M, and L segments. We also developed an 51 accompanying bioinformatic pipeline that performs reference-guided assembly of 52 hantavirus genomes, consensus generation, variant calling, and DVG classification 53 using the newly developed ORCHID classification pipeline. We applied this approach to 54 diverse Puumala virus strains from infected cell cultures and bank voles, to 55 representative Old World and New World orthohantaviruses, and to highly pathogenic 56 New World viruses in vivo. In all cases we were able to accurately reconstruct full 57 hantavirus genomes. Notably, we found that hantavirus populations contain highly 58 abundant DVGs and conserved L segment deletions, whereas the S and M segments 59 remained largely intact. Together, this work provides a low-cost, broadly applicable and 60 easily customisable workflow for hantavirus genomics and reveals DVGs as a 61 previously unrecognized feature of hantavirus populations. 62 63 IMPORTANCE 64 Hantaviruses cause severe and often fatal human diseases, and their diversity and low 65 viral loads make them hard to sequence, which limits surveillance and outbreak 66 investigation. We describe a simple, universal but customisable, low-cost nanopore 67 sequencing workflow that recovers complete genome segments, including the full-length 68 L segment, from cell culture and animal tissues across the entire Orthohantavirus 69 genus. Using this approach, we report the first evidence of defective viral genomes in 70 hantaviruses. These truncated genomes arise mainly from the L segment, which 71 encodes the viral polymerase, and are formed at conserved genomic regions. Defective 72 viral genomes can modulate viral replication, innate immune activation, and persistence 73 in other viruses. Their presence in hantaviruses raises new questions about polymerase 74 function, tolerance in reservoir hosts, and immune-mediated disease in humans. Our 75 framework offers a practical tool for hantavirus genomics and a foundation for 76 investigating how defective genomes shape hantavirus infection. 77 3 INTRODUCTION 78 Orthohantaviruses (family Hantaviridae, class Bunyaviricetes) are zoonotic segmented 79 negative-sense RNA viruses that are naturally found in small mammal species, 80 including rodents, shrews, moles and bats (1). Human infections occur primarily through 81 inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected animal hosts and can cause severe 82 disease, including haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and nephropathia 83 epidemica (NE) caused by Old World hantaviruses primarily in Eurasia and hantavirus 84 cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by New World hantaviruses in the Americas 85 (2, 3). Case fatality rates for hantavirus diseases vary significantly depending on the 86 infecting virus species (4): it ranges from <1% for Puumala virus (PUUV), the causative 87 agent for NE, to up to 15% for HFRS-causing Old World hantaviruses such as Hantaan 88 virus (HTNV) in East Asia and Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) in eastern Europe, and 89 over 30% for HCPS-causing New World hantaviruses such as Andes virus (ANDV) and 90 Sin Nombre virus (SNV). 91 Hantaviruses have small tripartite negative-sense RNA genomes comprising the small 92 (S), medium (M) and large (L) genome segments, encoding only 4-5 viral proteins (5). 93 The S segment encodes the nucleoprotein (NP) and in some cases a non-structural 94 (NS) protein, the M segment encodes the glycoprotein precursor (GPC) which is co- 95 translationally cleaved into the Gn and Gc glycoproteins, and the L segment encodes 96 the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The genetic sequence divergence at the 97 amino acid level is significant across the hantavirus family (up to 75%) and even within 98 a species (up to 24%) (6). Low viral RNA copy numbers in clinical and rodent samples, 99 and natural RNA degradation outside of infected hosts makes obtaining complete 100 coverage of hantavirus genomes challenging (7, 8). Current state-of-the-art sequencing 101 approaches include metagenome sequencing, tiled amplicon sequencing and hybrid 102 capture-based sequencing, which all require extensive optimisation and large numbers 103 of probes (9–12). Existing long-read amplicon-based sequencing approaches often 104 include single amplicons for the smaller segments, but to date, there are no established 105 protocols to reliably capture the entire L segment in a single amplicon. In addition, while 106 these methods can provide full genome coverage sequencing and provide consensus 107 sequences of viruses, they do not accurately reflect the genetic makeup of any given 108 virus population. In reality, virus populations are highly heterogeneous and contain large 109 proportions of defective viral genomes (DVGs) consisting of genome truncations, 110 duplications and recombinations (13). analysis_zh.background: 正汉坦病毒es 是人畜共患的三段负链 RNA 病毒,可导致严重的人类疾病,由于病毒载量低且多样性高,测序困难。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者设计了一套针对保守末端的通用逆转录引物组合,并为每个片段设计了单一的物种特异性引物,实现了完整S、M和L片段的扩增;一个生物信息学流程执行参考引导组装、共识序列生成、变异检测以及缺陷病毒基因组(DVG)分类(ORCHID)。
analysis_zh.results: 在细胞培养和田鼠的 普马拉病毒 株系以及旧世界和新世界的 汉坦病毒 中应用此框架后,重建了完整基因组;检测到大量缺陷病毒基因组(DVG),主要表现为L片段的保守缺失,而S和M片段保持完整。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该工作流程提供了一种低成本、广泛适用的 汉坦病毒 基因组学方法,并揭示缺陷病毒基因组(DVG)是一项此前未被识别的特征,为研究其对复制、免疫和疾病的影响奠定基础。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告。

papers.title: Vascular Programs in Emerging and Re-Emerging RNA Virus Infections: Comparative Lessons from SARS-CoV-2, Flaviviruses, and Hantaviruses.
papers.abstract: Emerging and re-emerging RNA viruses frequently present with clinical phenotypes that extend beyond classical organ tropism and include vascular leakage, platelet dysregulation, coagulation imbalance, microvascular injury, and thromboinflammation. SARS-CoV-2, flaviviruses, and hantaviruses provide three complementary models of virus-induced vascular disease. This narrative review compares these viruses through a shared endothelial-coagulative framework and proposes four partially overlapping vascular programs: endothelial activation, endothelial barrier failure, coagulation activation, and platelet quantitative or qualitative dysfunction. These programs are intended as a conceptual synthesis of convergent clinical, pathological, and experimental evidence rather than as a quantitative classification system. The framework is used not only to organize known mechanisms, but also to generate testable predictions for cross-virus biomarker panels, organ-specific endothelial models, and phenotype-guided clinical studies. Severe COVID-19 illustrates inflammation-driven endothelial activation, platelet-leukocyte interactions, complement amplification, NETosis, and immunothrombosis. Within the flavivirus group, DENV is used as the principal model for systemic vascular leakage, thrombocytopenia, and hemorrhagic risk; selected non-dengue flaviviruses illustrate how shared endothelial, platelet, and coagulation modules are redirected toward placental dysfunction (ZIKV), neuroinvasion (WNV and JEV), or hepatic failure and coagulopathy (YFV). Hantavirus infections provide a distinctive model of capillary leak syndrome in which non-lytic endothelial infection, immune-mediated injury, and permeability signaling converge on renal and pulmonary microvascular beds. A comparative view suggests that thrombotic, hemorrhagic, and leaky phenotypes are not mutually exclusive categories, but different outcomes of overlapping vascular programs shaped by viral tropism, vascular-bed specialization, immune activation, and host susceptibility.

papers.title: Can Hantavirus cruise into the next pandemic?
papers.abstract: Despite concerns arising from a recent ship-associated outbreak on the M/V Hondius cruise, current evidence suggests that Andes virus (ANDV) poses a low pandemic risk. Nevertheless, viral evolution, ecological changes, and reservoir host dynamics could drive future emergence of ANDV, underscoring the need for improved surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccine preparedness.

papers.title: Vaccines Against Hantavirus Infections: A Systematic Literature Review.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hantaviruses infections are responsible for a hemorrhagic fever with renal and cardiopulmonary syndrome with case-fatality rates up to 50%. While inactivated vaccines are already available in China and South Korea, several additional candidate vaccines are under development. This systematic review summarizes the current clinical evidence on immunogenicity and short-term safety of vaccines targeting different hantavirus strains. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic literature search was carried out to identify randomized and nonrandomized trials of any phase. Data were synthesized narratively within strata defined by vaccine platform, target virus, assay, immunogenicity and safety. Results: Ten trials on 961 adults were included: four single-arm trials on the inactivated vaccine and six early-phase DNA-vaccine trials. One month after last dose, the inactivated vaccine achieved neutralizing seropositivity by PRNT 50 in 45.1% of the tested subjects after two priming doses and 55.7% after three, while the corresponding binding-antibody values measured by IFA were 87.3% and 95.7%. Among DNA vaccines, homologous responses reached 100% against HTNV and 83.3% against PUUV with monovalent constructs, whereas dual responses to the bivalent construct were registered in 33.3% and 77.8% of the subjects, when measured through PRNT 50 and PsVNA 50 , respectively. One serious adverse event occurred, most likely unrelated to vaccination. Conclusions: No serious safety signal was identified, although safety remains insufficiently characterized. Measured immunogenicity depends as much on the assay as on the vaccine, and, in the absence of a validated correlate of protection, it cannot be read as a clinical benefit. Future research should prioritize validated correlates of protection and innovative trial designs adapted to low-incidence diseases.

papers.title: Host-Virus Immune Interactions in Andes Virus Infection: Implications for Human-to-Human Transmission, Pathogenesis, and Public Health.
papers.abstract: The Andes virus (ANDV, Orthohantavirus , andesense) is unique among hantaviruses in that it may transfer from person to person and cause severe vascular damage. The evidence on host-virus immunological interactions and their importance in disease progression, transmission, and public health is compiled in this narrative review. ANDV mostly affects pulmonary endothelial cells and does not result in widespread cell loss. Rather, the loss of vascular barrier integrity is caused by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling, Ras homolog family member A (RhoA) activation, breakdown of vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin, hypoxia-related pathways, and mediators produced from infected pericytes. Additionally, the virus interferes with early antiviral defenses involving protein kinase R (PKR), TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1)-interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS), and retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)/melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5). The intensity or outcome of the disease has been associated with increased interleukin-6 (IL-6), altered complement activity, thrombocytopenia, neutralizing-antibody reactions, and specific host genetic variations; nevertheless, significant T-cell activation does not necessarily correspond with viral clearance. Blood and a number of mucosal and secretory samples have been found to contain ANDV ribonucleic acid (RNA), albeit RNA discovery by itself does not prove the presence of an infectious virus. Epidemiological evidence indicates that Secondary transmission is rare and mostly linked to extended close or intimate contact. Genomic sequencing, when paired with epidemiological evidence, can shed light on transmission chains. Recent outbreaks linked to travel further emphasize the significance of worldwide surveillance and coordinated contact tracing. Prospective studies integrating genomic analysis, serial virological sampling, and standardized exposure evaluation are required to more effectively define the infectious phase and transmission patterns.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The Andes virus (ANDV) uniquely transmits between humans and causes severe vascular injury. Main directions: The review compiles host‑virus immune interactions, endothelial damage mechanisms, viral immune evasion, and public‑health implications. Current state: ANDV mainly infects pulmonary endothelial cells without widespread cell loss, disrupting vascular barriers via VEGF, RhoA, VE‑cadherin loss, hypoxia pathways, and pericyte mediators. papers.title: Rising spillover risk: Lessons from the Andes hantavirus outbreak.
papers.abstract: The unprecedented expansion of human activity boundaries is turning spillover from a chance event into a foreseeable ecological and epidemiological certainty. Using the 2026 Andes hantavirus cruise ship outbreak as an entry point, this study examines it within a broader driver framework: nearly all emerging infectious disease events in humans in recent decades have originated from wildlife transmission; under climate-change and land-use scenarios, approximately 3139 mammal species are projected to aggregate in new combinations by 2070, causing an estimated 4000 cross-species viral transmission events. The rapid expansion of tourism into ecologically fragile regions - sub-Antarctic waters, the deep sea, and primary forests - the persistence of habitat fragmentation and animal trade, and the reshaping of wildlife distribution and vector dynamics by extreme climate events together constitute "novel contact amplifiers" that accelerate contact at the human-animal-environment interface. Robotics, artificial intelligence, autonomous driving, and automated logistics are extending human activities into previously inaccessible regions, yet they remain almost entirely absent from current spillover risk assessments. The limitations of cruise ship medical systems - whose core capacity lies in "recognize, isolate, stabilize, and transfer" rather than definitive diagnosis and treatment - were fully exposed in this event. From a One Health perspective, this paper proposes that responses to spillover risk must shift from passive reaction to proactive interface governance, incorporate technology-driven increases in contact frequency into prevention and control frameworks, and advance cornerstone strategies such as broad-spectrum vaccines and broad-spectrum antiviral drugs at the basic research level.

analysis.background: Spillover events are becoming increasingly predictable as human activity expands into new ecological zones, raising concerns for future zoonotic outbreaks.
analysis.methods: The authors use the 2026 Andes hantavirus cruise‑ship outbreak as a case study examined within a broader driver framework of wildlife‑origin emerging infections.
analysis.results: Modelled climate‑change and land‑use scenarios predict that by 2070 about 3,139 mammal species will form new assemblages, potentially generating ~4,000 cross‑species viral transmission events.
analysis.contribution: The paper identifies “novel contact amplifiers” such as tourism, habitat fragmentation, and extreme climate events, and calls for proactive One Health governance and development of broad‑spectrum vaccines and antivirals.
analysis.limitations: The analysis notes that emerging technologies (e.g., robotics, AI) are omitted from current risk assessments and that cruise‑ship medical capacities are limited; conclusions are based on an abstract‑only overview.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Spillover risk is rising as human activity encroaches on wildlife habitats. Methods: A case‑study analysis of the 2026 Andes hantavirus cruise‑ship outbreak within a driver framework was performed. Results: Projections indicate ~3,139 mammal species will form new combinations by 2070, leading to an estimated 4,000 cross‑species viral transmissions. Contribution: The study highlights novel contact amplifiers and urges proactive One Health governance plus broad‑spectrum vaccine and antiviral development. Limitations: Emerging technologies are absent from risk models, cruise‑ship medical systems are limited, and the paper is based on abstract‑only evidence.

papers.title_zh: 上升的溢出风险:安第斯病毒 汉坦病毒 爆发的经验教训。

analysis_zh.background: 随着人类活动向新生态区扩展,跨种传播事件的可预测性日益提升,令人担忧未来的动物源性疫情爆发。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者以2026年安第斯病毒 汉坦病毒 邮轮暴发为案例,置于更广泛的野生动物来源新发感染驱动因素框架中进行研究。
analysis_zh.results: 模型预测的气候变化和土地利用情景显示,至2070年约有3,139种哺乳动物将形成新群落,可能产生约4,000起跨物种病毒传播事件。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本文指出旅游、栖息地碎片化和极端气候事件等“新型接触放大器”,并呼吁采取主动的 One Health 治理以及研发广谱疫苗和抗病毒药物。
analysis_zh.limitations: 分析指出,新兴技术(如机器人、人工智能)未纳入当前风险评估,且邮轮医疗能力有限;结论基于仅摘要概览。

papers.title: Differential PCDH1 usage by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal hantaviruses.
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus are hantaviruses associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), but their cellular entry receptors have not been defined. We used replication-competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing hantavirus Gn/Gc glycoprotein complexes to compare entry by these viruses, the Old World rodent-borne Dabieshan virus and Tigray virus, and the shrew-borne Cao Bang virus and Amga virus. All six Gn/Gc complexes supported infection of primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells, with virus-specific efficiencies and kinetics. Genetic ablation of protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) reduced infection mediated by Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus Gn/Gc in human osteosarcoma and endothelial cells, whereas PCDH1 re-expression restored susceptibility. Both viruses were captured by a soluble PCDH1 protein comprising the first two extracellular cadherin domains. Infection was also inhibited by a soluble decoy containing the first cadherin domain, and by an antibody specific to that domain, indicating that the first PCDH1 cadherin domain mediates viral engagement. Black Creek Canal Gn/Gc-bearing rVSVs incorporated less Gn/Gc and showed lower apparent capture by PCDH1 than Laguna Negra virus and Andes virus Gn/Gc-bearing particles, even after normalization for glycoprotein abundance. In contrast, PCDH1 depletion did not detectably alter infection mediated by the other four hantavirus Gn/Gc complexes. Thus, Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus use PCDH1 for efficient entry but differ in apparent receptor engagement and responses to PCDH1-directed inhibitors, whereas all six viruses are potently neutralized by the broadly reactive Gn/Gc-directed antibody ADI-42898. IMPORTANCE: The receptors used by many medically important hantaviruses remain incompletely characterized. Using BSL2-compatible rVSVs bearing hantavirus glycoproteins, we show that Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus, two hantaviruses associated with human cardiopulmonary disease, used protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) for efficient entry into human cells. PCDH1-directed inhibitors blocked infection, but the two viruses differed in apparent receptor engagement and inhibitor sensitivity, showing that PCDH1 usage is not uniform even among closely related viruses. Gn/Gc complexes from four additional divergent hantaviruses carried by shrews and Old World rodents infected primary human endothelial cells without detectable PCDH1 dependence, emphasizing the need to identify alternative entry factors. A broadly reactive antibody neutralized every virus in the study panel, supporting conserved viral glycoprotein surfaces as therapeutic targets when receptor usage is diverse or unknown.

analysis_zh.background: Laguna Negra 和 Black Creek Canal 汉坦病毒 病毒导致 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,但其细胞进入受体尚未知晓。
analysis_zh.methods: 使用携带 汉坦病毒 Gn/Gc 复合体的可复制 rVSV 感染原代人肺微血管内皮细胞和人骨肉瘤细胞;对 PCDH1 进行基因敲除或重新表达,并加入可溶性 PCDH1 区域和抗体。
analysis_zh.results: 所有六种 Gn/Gc 复合体均能感染内皮细胞,但 PCDH1 缺失降低了 Laguna Negra 和 Black Creek Canal 病毒的感染;可溶性 PCDH1 及第一钙黏蛋白结构域抗体阻断了进入;Black Creek Canal 的 Gn/Gc 蛋白掺入的糖蛋白较少,且对 PCDH1 的捕获能力较低;其余四种 汉坦病毒 病毒则不依赖 PCDH1。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究将 PCDH1 确认作为两种与汉坦病毒心肺综合征相关的 汉坦病毒 病毒的高效进入受体,展示了相关病毒在受体利用上的差异,并表明一种广谱中和抗体能够针对所有检测病毒。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅有摘要数据可得;未报告详细的样本量、采集地点和宿主物种。
